title: Oil Slides Toward $90 as US-Iran Pause Holds for Third Night; Iran Says It Controls Hormuz, Won't Seek Talks
subhead: A US-Iran pause on strikes has held for a third night, sending oil prices plunging 7-9% after Monday's spike above $108, even as Tehran insists it controls the Strait of Hormuz and is not seeking talks. The market is pricing a diplomatic off-ramp that Iran's rhetoric has yet to confirm.

sections.heading: Oil Crashes as US-Iran Diplomatic Pause Holds
sections.body: The sharpest oil-market reversal in weeks played out as the US and Iran paused strikes for a third consecutive night while mediators report progress on a diplomatic opening, per today's reporting. Oil prices plunged 7-9% on the de-escalation hopes, with prices 'sliding below $90' according to one headline read. That marks a dramatic swing from Monday, when Brent topped $108 and WTI cleared $103 after Oman postponed GCC-Iran talks and Saudi Arabia's key pipeline stayed shut, as reported by Trading News and MSN. The whiplash — a spike above $108 followed by a 7-9% crash within 48 hours — shows how fully the market has been trading the war's diplomatic trajectory rather than the underlying supply damage, which remains unresolved with millions of barrels a day still off the market.
sections.whyItMatters: The violent round-trip reveals a market dominated by headline diplomacy, not physical barrels. Any collapse of the pause will re-spike prices faster than the slide down.

sections.heading: Iran Says It Controls Hormuz, Won't Seek Talks — Contradicting Pause Narrative
sections.body: The diplomatic picture is muddier than the market's rally suggests. Iran claims control of the Strait of Hormuz and says it is not seeking talks after the US bombing halt, according to today's headlines — directly at odds with President Trump saying Iran 'wants to reach a deal', as Reuters reported Monday. The mechanism for a settlement — an Oman-mediated or GCC-Iran meeting on Hormuz — has been postponed, with Oman's foreign minister confirming the delay, per CBS News' live tracking. Hormuz shipping traffic remains below its 10-day average even at the weekend, data cited by Ariana News shows. A pause in strikes is not a ceasefire, and Tehran's public posture signals it sees the halt as a battlefield outcome to leverage, not a prelude to concessions.
sections.whyItMatters: When Iran's official line and Washington's read diverge this openly, the 'progress' mediators cite may amount to little more than an agreed silence. The market may be over-discounting re-escalation risk.

sections.heading: Saudi Pipeline Stays Dark as Iraqi Drones and Houthis Keep Targeting Oil Sites
sections.body: Saudi Arabia's East-West Petroline — its only pipeline bypassing Hormuz — remains shut after Iraq-origin drones destroyed the line on September 10, a strike that also sent US diesel to a record with no backup route, per MSN reporting. Saudi forces intercepted additional Iranian-backed militia drones targeting oil facilities as regional attacks spread to Jordan and Iraq, today's headlines report. Yemen's Houthis — Iran's main regional proxy — launched new strikes on Saudi Arabia, with 13 civilians injured in attacks on three Saudi cities, according to Times of India's live updates. With the bypass line dark — roughly 7 million barrels a day of capacity still shut in, per Trading News — Saudi Arabia's ability to export while Hormuz is contested is materially impaired, and the world's spare-cushion has narrowed further.
sections.whyItMatters: The dual chokepoint pressure — Hormuz contested and the Petroline bypass destroyed — is structural supply damage that a diplomatic pause does not repair. Even a 'deal' leaves Saudi export capacity crippled for months.

sections.heading: US Uses Snapback to Block Iran's Nuclear Chief From IAEA Meeting
sections.body: Washington escalated the nuclear dimension of the standoff by blocking Iran's nuclear chief Mohammad Eslami from attending the IAEA General Conference in Vienna, using the UN snapback mechanism to deny him entry, according to Reuters and Khaleej Times. Iran accused the US of 'bullying political pressure,' with senior nuclear agency official Behrouz Kamalvandi condemning the move, Deccan Chronicle and TeleSUR reported. Eslami had attended and spoken at the same gathering last year as an IAEA member state. Denying a member's senior official a seat at the agency's annual meeting is an unusual step that hardens Tehran's position just as the pause in strikes opens room for diplomacy — and it follows the IAEA's prior referral of Tehran to the UN Security Council this month.
sections.whyItMatters: Banning Iran's nuclear chief from the IAEA is a deliberate hardening signal that undercuts the softer 'pause' narrative — it tells Tehran that Washington intends to keep maximum pressure on the nuclear file even while probing de-escalation on the military track.

sections.heading: BRICS Summit Delivers United Front Against the US War — With Energy Backdrop
sections.body: Leaders of emerging powers including Russia and Iran projected a united front at Modi's New Delhi BRICS summit, issuing a joint statement targeting the US-launched war in the Middle East and Washington's sanctions, BusinessMirror reported. Putin called for BRICS to build a new platform for global growth 'free from Western rules,' and deepened Moscow-New Delhi ties, per Reuters. The energy wiring beneath this politics is tightening: India supplied around 70% of Russia's oil-product imports in August, per the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), as Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries push Moscow to import finished fuels. India's refined-fuel exports to Russia surge to 70% even as its crude imports from Moscow fell 24%, MSN reports — a refinery-arbitrage relationship that deepens the Delhi-Moscow axis independent of the war's military course.
sections.whyItMatters: The BRICS joint statement formalizes an anti-Western energy-trade bloc at the same moment India becomes Russia's critical fuel supplier. Russia's war-driven dependency on Indian refined products is cementing a trade architecture Washington's sanctions cannot easily sever.

sections.heading: Critical Minerals: US Invests, But China Still Grips the Chain
sections.body: A new report from the REEII (published via Reuters, Sept 14) finds that despite US government initiatives, China remains dominant in the supply of critical minerals crucial for clean energy. US investment has yet to translate into supply-chain independence for lithium, rare earths and battery inputs, even as the IEA projects critical-minerals demand to grow by more than 6% a year on energy-transition buildout, per an Americas-focused analysis cited in Dialogo Americas. The report lands as the Western critical-minerals push accelerates — Greenland's mining venture formed a strategic advisory board to advance its rare-earths project, Business Insider reports — but the structural gap between Western capital and Chinese processing capacity remains the defining constraint.
sections.whyItMatters: For all the strategic-rhetoric around 'de-risking,' the REEII finding is a blunt reality check: Western investment is flowing, but China still controls the midstream processing that determines who actually wins the critical-minerals contest.

bottomLine: Energy markets spent the day swinging violently on the US-Iran pause — oil plunging 7-9% and sliding toward $90 after Monday's spike above $108 — but the rally rests on diplomacy that Tehran publicly rejects. Iran says it controls Hormuz and won't seek talks even as Trump claims Iran wants a deal, while the Saudi Petroline bypass stays dark with ~7 million bpd shut in and Washington simultaneously hardens the nuclear track by barring Iran's nuclear chief from the IAEA. The BRICS summit's united front and India's surge to covering 70% of Russia's fuel imports underline that the war's real durable consequence — a re-wired, non-Western energy-trade architecture — is proceeding in parallel to the battlefield. If today's pause is real, it buys time but repairs none of the physical supply damage; if it unravels, the price spike that follows will be steeper than Monday's.
